title: Beauty Is Vain
text:
While roses are red,

while lilies are so white,

will a woman exalt her features

only to offer delight?

She is not as sweet as the rose,

the lily is prouder and pale,

and if she were like red or white

she would be only one among many.


If she reddens in love's summer

or in its winter grows dry,

if she displays her beauty

or hides behind a false blush,

whether she dresses in white or red silk,

and stands crooked or straight as wood,

time always wins the race

that hides us beneath a shroud.




"Beauty is vain"

The Prince's Progress and Other Poems, 1866
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's plain warning that beauty, ornament, and posture all lose to time.

title: A Green Cornfield
text:
The earth was green, the sky was blue:

I saw and heard, on a sunny morning,

a lark hanging between the two,

a singing shape above the grain;


and just below, in cheerful measure,

white butterflies were beating their wings,

and still the lark rose higher,

silently sank, and rose to sing.


The cornfield spread its tender green

around my steps;

I knew there was a hidden nest,

a secret audience among a million stalks.


And as I paused to hear its voice,

while the sunny moment slipped away,

perhaps its lover sat enchanted,

listening to the ending of that song.




"A Green Cornfield"

Goblin Market and Other Poems, 1875
editorial_note: The translation keeps the pastoral scene centered on the suspended lark and its hidden listener.

title: The One Certainty
text:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher,

all things are vanity.

The eye and ear cannot be filled

with images and sounds.

Like the first dew, or the pale,

sudden breath of wind,

or like grass torn from the mountain,

so too is man,

floating between hope and fear:

how small his joys are,

how slight, how shadowed,

until all things end

in the slow dust of oblivion.

Today is the same as yesterday,

tomorrow must become one of them;

and there is nothing new under the sun:

until Time's ancient race has run,

the old thorn will grow on its weary trunk,

and morning will be cold, and twilight gray.




"The One Certainty"
editorial_note: The translation preserves Rossetti's Ecclesiastes-like certainty of repetition, frailty, and dust.

title: I Survive
